name: Kubera
role: God of wealth and king of the yakshas, guardian of the north
summary: Kubera is the Hindu god of wealth and the king of the yakshas, spirits who guard hidden treasure. He rules from Alaka in the Himalayas and guards the northern direction.
about: Kubera first appears in the Atharvaveda, and early texts describe him as lord of spirits and hidden things. Later texts, including the Manusmriti, the epics and the Puranas, make him a respectable lokapala, a world guardian who is patron of merchants and guardian of the north. In the Ramayana, Brahma gave him the Pushpaka Vimana and the treasures called nidhis, and his half-brother Ravana took Lanka and the flying chariot from him. He then lived in Alaka in the Himalayas. He is usually shown as a stocky figure with a big belly, carrying a mace or money bag. A temple tradition says he lent money to Venkateswara at Tirupati. Buddhists know him as Vaishravana, one of the Four Heavenly Kings, called Bishamonten in Japan, and Jains name a yaksha of Mallinatha after him.
kidSummary: Kubera is the god of wealth, who keeps hidden treasures safe. Stories say he once owned a golden flying chariot called Pushpaka Vimana. At Tirupati people say he lent money to Lord Venkateswara, so visitors give gifts to help repay it.

story.title: The golden city
story.text: In the Ramayana, Kubera is the king of the yakshas and lord of wealth. Brahma gave him the right to guard treasures and also gave him a flying chariot called Pushpaka Vimana.

story.title: The flying chariot
story.text: Pushpaka was a wonderful flying vehicle. Texts say it was made by the divine builder Vishvakarma and could carry its owner across the sky.

story.title: Ravana takes Lanka
story.text: Kubera's half-brother Ravana took Lanka and the chariot. Kubera then moved to Alaka, a city among the Himalayas, and ruled from there.

story.title: The chariot comes back
story.text: After the war in Lanka, Rama is said to have returned the Pushpaka to Kubera, so the chariot went back to its first owner.

story.title: A loan for a wedding
story.text: A Tirupati tradition says Kubera lent wealth to Venkateswara for his marriage. Devotees give offerings there to help repay the loan.

teaches: Wealth should be guarded and used with care
Sharing and giving matter more than owning
Honest effort and gratitude go together with prosperity
emblems: Nara (man or water spirit) as mount

facts.text: The name of the Chinese god Nezha is a shortened form of Nalakuvara, the name of one of Kubera's sons in Indian texts.
The Shatapatha Brahmana calls him lord of thieves, but the Manusmriti recasts him as a respectable world guardian and patron of merchants.
Puranic descriptions show Kubera as a stocky dwarf with a big belly, and some texts give him three legs, eight teeth and one eye.
In Tibet, a mongoose in Kubera's hand stands for victory over the nagas, the guardians of treasure, and Buddhist images of him usually include one.
He is called Ekaksipingala, meaning one yellow eye, after a story in which he looked jealously at Shiva and Parvati and lost an eye.
In Kalidasa's poem Meghaduta, a yaksha who serves King Kubera is exiled for a year for neglecting his duties and asks a passing cloud to carry a message to his wife in Alaka.
Valmiki says the Pushpaka Vimana was built by Vishvakarma for Brahma, who gave it to Kubera; Ravana later seized it.
In the Bhagavata Purana, Kubera's sons Nalakuvara and Manigriva are cursed by the sage Narada to stand as twin arjuna trees until the child Krishna frees them.

A Tirupati tradition says Kubera lent Venkateswara money for his marriage to Padmavati, so devotees fill the temple's donation pot to help repay it; the story also links Kubera with Lakshmi as Kubera Lakshmi.
In Buddhism he is Vaishravana, one of the Four Heavenly Kings, guarding the north, and in Japan he is Bishamonten of the Seven Lucky Gods.
The Puranas make Kubera a son of Vishrava, so Ravana, Kumbhakarna, Vibhishana and Shurpanakha are his half-siblings, while the Mahabharata calls Vishrava his brother, making Ravana his nephew.
Kubera is called Nara-vahana, one whose mount is a man; the Vishnudharmottara Purana says this rider-mount is the state itself, dressed in gold.
In the epics, as a world guardian Kubera rides the elephant Sarvabhauma, and in his garden Chaitraratha the leaves are said to be jewels, with a lovely lake called Nalini inside it.
In the Vishnudharmottara Purana, the treasures Padma and Shankha stand beside Kubera in human form, with their heads rising from a lotus and a conch.
Jains honour Kubera as Sarvanubhuti, the attendant yaksha of the 19th Tirthankara, Mallinatha, and picture him with features such as four faces, rainbow colours and eight arms.
A Purana tale says vain Kubera invited Shiva to a feast to show off his wealth; Shiva sent little Ganesha, who ate everything, and only a handful of roasted rice offered with love satisfied him.
In the Ramayana, Brahma rewarded Kubera's severe penance with the post of world guardian, the world's riches called nidhis, equality with the gods and the Pushpaka Vimana.
Kubera's city Alaka means curl-city, and it also goes by Prabha, splendour, Vasudhara, bejewelled, and Vasusthali, abode of treasures.
The Puranas say Kubera's wife Bhadra, also called Riddhi, bore three sons, Nalakubara, Manigriva and Mayuraja, and a daughter named Minakshi, meaning fish-eyed.
In Buddhist legends Kubera is equated with Pancika, whose wife Hariti is a symbol of abundance, and their images are so alike that it can be very hard to tell them apart.
Kubera is called the guardian of travellers as well as the treasurer of the gods, and the yakshas who serve him guard the jewels of the earth.
The Padma Purana says Kubera prayed to Shiva for many years and was granted kingship of the yakshas, and the epics often call him Shiva's friend.

quiz.q: What did Brahma give Kubera in the Ramayana?
quiz.why: Brahma gave him the flying chariot Pushpaka and other gifts.

quiz.q: Which half-brother took Lanka from Kubera?
quiz.why: The Ramayana says his half-brother Ravana took Lanka.
Kubera is the guardian of the north.

quiz.q: Who did Kubera lend money to, in a Tirupati tradition?
quiz.why: The tradition says he lent money to Venkateswara for his marriage.

quiz.q: What is Kubera called in Japan?
quiz.why: Japanese Buddhism knows him as Bishamonten.
